data.title: Warsh optimistic about US resilience
data.description:
‘HANGING IN THERE’: Global central banks opted for ‘a synchronous tightening in monetary policy,’ while benefiting from an AI ‘investment surge’,’ the Fed chair said

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh voiced optimism yesterday about US economic strength and surprise about how well global economies have been “hanging in there” amid continued energy shocks and tighter monetary policy to fight inflation.

He said the US and many other economies were benefiting from an “investment surge” driven by artificial intelligence (AI) but broadening to other sectors, creating a near-term demand shock that was putting upward pressure on inflation.

“I came out of meetings here yesterday and today and it’s hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices,” Warsh said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.

With inflation a “common challenge,” Warsh said global central banks undertook “a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world, and that means there’s no free riders.”

In the US “we made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago,” he said in a reference to the Fed’s interest-rate hike last month.

However, in keeping with his style since taking the reins as Fed chief in May, he gave no preview about whether he feels more interest-rate hikes would be needed, or when.

“I don’t prejudge meetings,” Warsh added in the discussion with IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva. “I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.”

Financial markets have taken those remarks on board and are betting the Fed would wait until December to raise rates.

That remained true even after reports this week showed two different measures of inflation running higher than expected and heading in the wrong direction from the Fed’s 2 percent goal.

Warsh was optimistic about the impact of AI on economic growth and productivity in the medium-term, even as he said it would be a “very bumpy” path toward what he expected would be faster productivity growth in the “real economy” that would bolster wealth.

“It’s obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it’s going to hit the supply side of the economy,” he said. “We don’t know in the next 12 or 18 months its effect on employment, but if you believe like I believe, which is it will make economies and countries that put it to good use more productive, that it’s going to make it so that we will have more wealth, then that has to be a very good thing.”

A task force convened to advise the Fed on the impact of AI on productivity and jobs would hold a “field hearing” in San Francisco on Nov. 16, he said, in what would be a first public peek at the group’s work.

Warsh said that central bankers meeting in Bangkok had a common vision to safeguard price stability and were taking action to back that view, which was giving “confidence to businesses and households that’s so important for growth to continue.”

“I believe optimistically — you might think naively — at least in the United States, we’re going to come out of this stronger with a more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth,” Warsh said.

data.title: Nuclear power option still under consideration: Lai
data.description:
Taiwan should not rule out any energy source or abandon environmental sustainability in favor of ideology and short-term benefits, President William Lai (賴清德) said in an interview, calling for a “professional assessment” of whether nuclear power should be reintroduced into Taiwan’s energy mix.

In an online interview with influencer Yu Ting-hao (游庭皓) that aired yesterday, Lai reiterated his position on nuclear power.

SHIFT

Lai’s remarks marked a shift from the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP’s) longstanding opposition to nuclear power.

As premier from 2017 to 2019, Lai pushed for more gas-fired power capacity while sticking to the DPP’s nuclear free homeland ideology and rejected the idea of extending the service life of its nuclear power plants.

Taiwan phased out nuclear energy in May last year, fulfilling the nuclear free homeland pledge.

That occurred as Taiwan continued to rely on fossil fuels for more than 80 percent of its electricity mix, and questions remained over the electricity supply given the country’s development of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

In the interview with Yu, Lai said the Legislative Yuan has passed bills providing a legal basis for reintroducing nuclear power, and state-run Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) has been making preparations accordingly.

The government would begin work to resume nuclear power generation if nuclear safety and nuclear waste disposal issues can be resolved through a professional assessment in a way that wins public support, Lai said.

AI INDUSTRY

Meanwhile, asked how the government would balance efforts to develop the AI industry against the regulation of AI applications, Lai said it would promote the industry’s responsible development.

He cited the Artificial Intelligence Basic Act (人工智慧基本法), which took effect in January, saying it requires the government to uphold human autonomy, privacy, information security, fairness, non-discrimination, transparency and accountability while developing the AI industry.

To prevent AI from exacerbating the uneven distribution of wealth and resources between the high-tech and non-tech sectors, Lai said the government would provide NT$100 billion (US$3 billion) over eight years to help micro, small and medium-sized enterprises transform their businesses.

data.title: Tesla unveils a new rocket-powered Roadster
data.description:
JUST FOR SHOW: The new-generation sports car, which would not begin production until 2028, finally gives Tesla a showpiece after years of missed Roadster deadlines

Tesla unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered with rocket-style thrusters on Thursday and said it would start production in 2028, more than a decade after it first showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car.

The white two-seater vehicle, developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX, drove upside down on a ramp using a suction system, turned in the air and landed using built-in thrusters. Later in the event it used the thrusters to jump over a truck and other vehicles, twisting in the air during the maneuver.

Some watchers saw the collaboration as Musk drumming up interest in a merger of the two big companies he controls, an idea he has explored by discussing their overlap.

The reveal gives Tesla a showpiece car after years of missed Roadster deadlines, but it comes as the company shifts its focus to self-driving technology and robotics, and days before third-quarter results that analysts say matter more to investors.

“It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers,” Tesla investor Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster said on social media platform X.

“The Roadster event is the latest example of why Elon can’t wait to bring [Tesla] and [SpaceX] together,” Munster said.

Musk has played down the car’s importance to Tesla’s finances, describing it in 2023 as a “small potato situation” that would not “move the needle in a major way financially.”

However, the car still carries symbolic weight.

“Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker’s best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla’s new halo car,” Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said last month.

“That was the most insane product demo I’ve ever seen,” Tesla fan and investor Sawyer Merritt posted on X. “I just saw this in person, and I’m still asking how this wasn’t AI.”

Musk and other executives did not specify any target prices at Thursday’s event, although Tesla nearly a decade ago quoted a base price of US$200,000 for the vehicle.

Tesla’s reservation page for the Roadster after Thursday’s event showed a “Performance” version of the vehicle requiring a US$50,000 deposit and a “Thrust” version with “acceleration thrusters” requiring a US$250,000 deposit. A “Rocket” variant, which Tesla says is “invite only,” is described as a single-seat model with a “full flight system.”

The Roadster can accelerate from zero to 97kph in less than one second and can hit a top speed of more than 230mph (370kph), Tesla vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy said.

“Definitely much faster than that,” an excited Musk said. “I think you’ve got to crack halfway to the speed of sound.”

The Roadster can also travel more than 480km on a single charge. That is less than half of what Musk promised in 2017, when Tesla first revealed a prototype of the second-generation Roadster and said that deliveries would begin in 2020.

data.title: Global Tek forecasts double-digit growth
data.description:
Precision metal component maker Global Tek Fabrication Co Ltd (時碩工業) yesterday said it expects revenue this year to grow by at least a double-digit percentage from last year’s NT$4.97 billion (US$153.47 million), driven by volume shipments of key components for artificial intelligence (AI) liquid cooling systems.

Global Tek said it began ramping up production of key components last quarter from its factory in Wuxi, China.

The growth would also be fueled by rising demand for key components used in industrial applications and aerospace devices, the company said.

The momentum is expected to extend into next year, as the company has secured orders from several major cloud service providers in the US and Japan for liquid-cooling components, Global Tek president Donald Huang (黃亞興) said at an earnings conference in Taipei.

The products include microchannel cold plate components, universal quick-disconnect fittings, manifolds, valve bodies and other fluid-control components, Huang said.

The company is on track to boost AI-related and other emerging businesses to account for 20 percent of revenue in the first half of next year, from 6.2 percent in the first nine months of the year from thermal management systems for AI data centers, driven by new overseas orders for liquid-cooling systems, Huang said.

Global Tek mainly manufactures precision metal components for automotive, industrial and aerospace applications. Industrial applications components were the largest share of revenue during the first nine months of this year, accounting for 35 percent, company data showed. During the period, revenue expanded 23.41 percent annually to NT$4.64 billion.

Revenue is expected to remain robust this quarter, supported by steady demand from established automotive and industrial control businesses as well as growth in aerospace, AI, semiconductor equipment and humanoid robot applications, Huang said.

Shipments of precision components for a Chinese humanoid robot maker entered small-volume production this quarter and are expected to provide additional growth momentum next year, he said.

In Thailand, the company plans to inaugurate a new factory on Tuesday next week in Chonburi Province, where it also operates two other factories. The new factory is to enter volume production next year. In total, the company has invested NT$1 billion in the Thailand site, it said.

The Thailand factories produce components used in semiconductor equipment and robot-related applications, with aerospace aluminum alloy casting and stainless-steel precision casting to be added, Huang said.

The first phase of the aerospace aluminum alloy casting production line is expected to involve about NT$150 million in equipment investment, with mass production of the casting line scheduled to begin by the end of 2028, he said.

Global Tek would continue to expand capacity in its Wuxi, Suzhou and Xian factories, given the Chinese sites’ manufacturing advantages in terms of scale and costs, Huang said.

data.title: China proposes AI export curbs to manage security
data.description:
China proposed adding advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to its export-control list, potentially restricting overseas transfers of AI models and chip designs in an effort to keep closer control over homegrown advancements in a strategically important sector.

The draft proposal covers 23 AI technologies, including large language models, agents, chip designs and computing clusters. Restricted technologies would include model weights and source code for products exceeding certain performance thresholds.

Chinese AI startups have this summer made significant progress in closing the gap on US industry leaders. Models such as Moonshot (月之暗面) AI’s Kimi K3 and DeepSeek’s (深度求索) latest editions offer better pricing, and Chinese companies also favor the approach of sharing the weights — used to steer an AI system toward finding an answer — of their models to encourage developers to build on top of them. They are also increasingly looking for markets beyond China, with the likes of Z.AI Co (北京智譜華章科技) making their wares available on US cloud service providers such as Amazon Web Services.

The proposed export curbs are aimed at ensuring “the safety and controllability” of AI technology, a spokesperson for the Commerce Ministry said, citing the risk of misuse for attacking critical infrastructure, defense industries and core government systems by non-state actors or malicious entities.

“The Chinese government’s necessary management of these technologies aims to solidify the security baseline, prevent misuse and abuse, ensure that AI remains under human control, and promote international governance of AI,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

The proposal would restrict exports of core technology for models containing at least 2 trillion parameters — such as Kimi K3 or Alibaba Group Holding Ltd’s (阿里巴巴) Qwen3.8-Max — or ranking among the world’s top 10 on measures including performance, usage and safety. The curb would cover model weights, checkpoints, source code and architecture.

The new Chinese guidelines are likely to stoke uncertainty in an AI industry already grappling with strict content controls, a licensing regime and potential US sanctions.

AI models trained on China’s “core data,” as defined by relevant legislation such as the Data Security Law, would be banned from export, the proposal said. The Data Security Law describes state core data as “data concerning national security, the lifeline of the national economy, key public livelihoods and major public interests.”

Open-source technology and research already in the public domain would not be covered, and the government would provide streamlined procedures, such as automatic licensing, to exports involving open-source AI technologies. Beijing said the measures were not aimed at any particular country, region or entity.

China simultaneously imposed a temporary registration requirement for exports of the technologies covered by the proposal. The measure took effect yesterday and applies to transactions already underway but not completed, including intellectual-property transfers, overseas licensing and changes that place Chinese technology owners under foreign control.

data.title: Micron, union negotiate ‘sincerely’: Lai
data.description:
IN GOOD FAITH: Lai said he appreciates Micron’s commitment to Taiwan and that it would continue expanding its investment in the country, while also working with labor

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday called for US memory maker Micron Technology Inc and its workers to negotiate “sincerely” ahead of a possible strike by the company’s union in Taiwan.

Last week, a Taiwanese union representing workers at Micron said it had secured authorization from its members to strike over a dispute concerning the company’s bonus scheme, escalating a labor conflict at the chipmaker’s largest manufacturing hub.

Micron employs about 15,000 people in Taiwan and has said it invested more than NT$1.6 trillion (US$49.6 billion) in the country.

Speaking in Taichung at the opening of a new Micron advanced assembly and testing facility, Lai said he hoped the government and the private sector could work together to promote better communication between labor and management.

“We also hope both labor and management will uphold the spirit that fish need water and water needs fish, continuing to negotiate sincerely and in good faith to build the broadest possible consensus,” he added.

“Only by creating harmonious labor relations can both sides win, allowing employees to work with peace of mind and businesses to move steadily and go further,” he said.

Lai said he appreciated Micron’s commitment to Taiwan and hoped it would continue investing in the country, adding that Micron had secured government support for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) research and development.

Taiwan is a crucial production hub for Micron’s DRAM and HBM chips, which are used in artificial intelligence servers.

“Micron values its team members and remains committed to listening to their perspectives and engaging with them constructively,” the company said in a statement, when asked about Lai’s remarks.

Micron’s Taichung union said that it looked forward to the company engaging in “more substantive dialogue and negotiations” with them.

Micron president and chief operating officer Manish Bhatia made no mention of a possible strike action in his comments delivered shortly before Lai’s.

“We have already sold out all the capacity for 2027 that this factory will build and we expect high-bandwidth memory to grow faster than the rest of the DRAM industry all the way through 2028,” he said.

Last week, the two unions representing workers at Micron’s Taoyuan and Taichung operations said they hoped the company would put forward a concrete profit-sharing proposal for employees.

Mediation with the Taoyuan union ended without agreement last month, while the Taichung union remains in negotiations.

The unions are encouraging members to take a day off on Monday to join a rally in Taipei, which they said would not be a strike.

data.title: TAIEX slumps 3.41 percent to four-week low
data.description:
TECH STRAIN: TSMC and other major companies came under pressure as foreign investors pull back from chip and hardware stocks, an analyst said

Stocks in Taiwan slumped to a four-week low yesterday as hotter-than-expected US inflation rekindled concerns over interest rates and a global sell-off in technology shares intensified.

The benchmark TAIEX fell 1,655.96 points, or 3.41 percent, to close at 46,969.87, on turnover of NT$1.319 trillion (US$40.9 billion), Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE) data showed.

Foreign investors led the sell-off with net sales of NT$302.56 billion, while proprietary dealers sold a net NT$95.82 billion, largely through hedging transactions.

Investment trusts were the only net buyers, purchasing NT$28.3 billion of shares, TWSE data showed.

The decline came after US consumer prices rose 3.7 percent year-on-year last month, exceeding economists’ 3.6 percent forecast and raising concerns that the US Federal Reserve might raise interest rate again later this month or in December, putting further pressure on technology shares, whose valuations are sensitive to borrowing costs.

US technology stocks fell on Wall Street overnight, extending a decline in semiconductor shares to a sixth consecutive session. The sell-off spread across Asian markets yesterday, with South Korea’s KOSPI plunging 7.57 percent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 falling 4.9 percent.

The Fed is due to review its monetary policy on Oct. 27 and 28.

Taiwan’s market was particularly vulnerable to the downturn because of its heavy reliance on technology stocks. The electronics sector came under pressure, with major companies including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), MediaTek Inc (聯發科), Nanya Technology Corp (南亞科) and Delta Electronics Inc (台達電) among the hardest hit.

Cheng-tung Security Investment Consultant Co (承通證券) analyst Cheng Lung (陳龍) attributed the sell-off across Asia largely to foreign investors pulling back from semiconductor and hardware stocks.

“Investors are more concerned about the sustainability of artificial intelligence [AI] spending, as rising financing costs heighten the risks of a recession,” he said, advising against drawing direct comparisons between Taiwan and South Korea, which have different industrial structures.

Memory makers might be posting strong profits, but competition from Chinese rivals could erode their edge, Chen said.

Young Cheng Asset Management Co (永誠國際資產) analyst William Chen (陳威良) urged investors to stay calm amid market volatility, advising them to focus on the fundamentals of AI-related stocks and avoid making hasty decisions.

Concerns have mounted following Broadcom Inc CEO Hock Tan’s (陳福陽) warning that many AI investors do not understand what they are buying, comparing their behavior to casino gambling.

The sell-off in technology stocks intensified, as bond yields at US AI cloud provider CoreWeave Inc surged past 15 percent overnight, fueling unease over the financing risks of the AI boom.

data.title: Real wage growth in Taiwan hits an 11-year high
data.description:
Real wage growth in Taiwan reached an 11-year high in the first eight months of this year as robust exports supported earnings gains and inflation remained relatively moderate, helping improve purchasing power despite wide differences across industries, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said yesterday.

The average regular monthly wage rose 3.28 percent from a year earlier to NT$52,523 in August, while the total monthly wage — including bonuses, overtime pay and other compensation — climbed 6.64 percent to NT$69,520 on average, the agency said.

DGBAS Census Department Deputy Director Tan Wen-ling (譚文玲) attributed the gains to robust export growth, saying employment, regular wages and total earnings had all increased from a year earlier.

Overtime hours also continued to rise, she said.

“Wage increases and bonus payments, coupled with moderate inflation and government efforts to stabilize prices, have helped wages outpace consumer prices and support workers’ purchasing power,” Tan said.

However, the gap between average and median wages suggests that typical workers earn considerably less than the overall average.

The median regular monthly wage, a statistic that is less affected by outliers, rose 3.46 percent year-on-year to NT$41,353 in August, notably lower than the average wage of NT$52,523, DGBAS data showed.

Over the first eight months of the year, the median regular monthly wage increased 3.06 percent to NT$39,383, while the average regular monthly wage rose 2.94 percent to NT$49,110 and the total monthly wage increased 4.55 percent to NT$549,200.

After adjusting for inflation, the increase was 1.2 percent for the median regular monthly wage, 1.08 percent for the average regular monthly wage and 2.66 percent for the total monthly wage, which was an 11-year high, the agency said.

Wage growth also varied considerably by industry. Financial and insurance services recorded the strongest increase among major industries in the first eight months, with average regular monthly wages rising 5.85 percent from a year earlier to NT$75,313, the data showed.

Wholesale and retail trade wages increased 3.52 percent to NT$50,414 on average, while manufacturing wages rose 3.47 percent to NT$51,661 on average, it said.

Accommodation and food services recorded the weakest growth, with the average regular monthly wage rising just 0.4 percent to NT$38,871, underscoring the uneven distribution of wage gains across industries, the data showed.

Average working hours totaled 172.9 in August, up 0.5 hours from a year earlier, while average overtime hours increased by 0.1 hours to 8.9, reflecting sustained demand for labor amid strong demand for artificial intelligence hardware, the DGBAS said.

data.title: US to account for over 20% of LNG imports: minister
data.description:
US liquefied natural gas (LNG) is expected to account for more than 20 percent of Taiwan’s LNG imports this year, up from 10 percent last year, and rise to 25 percent by 2029, Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said yesterday.

If talks to purchase LNG from an Alaskan project proceed smoothly, supply could begin as early as 2032, potentially raising the US share in Taiwan’s LNG imports to 30 percent or more, Kung said.

Under a planned investment of up to US$4.4 billion in the project, CPC Corp, Taiwan (台灣中油) would purchase 6 million tonnes of LNG from Alaska annually once production begins, the ministry said.

As Taiwan’s natural gas demand continues to rise, with 25 additional large gas-fired power units expected to be added by 2035, the government needs to secure supplies in advance and diversify procurement sources to strengthen energy resilience, Kung said.

In addition, securing stable supplies through long-term contracts could help reduce price volatility in LNG imports, he said.

Alaska is also relatively close to Taiwan, with a shipping time of about 10 days, which could reduce transportation time and shipping risks, Kung said.

For the US$4.4 billion investment, the government has a preliminary plan and an investment ceiling, but the actual amount, equity stake and other terms still need to be determined through negotiations, he said.

Kung said he is confident in CPC’s ability to negotiate favorable investment terms, but declined to disclose pricing because of commercial confidentiality.

The source of funding for the investment would depend on the final investment structure, timetable and CPC’s financial position, and could include capital injections, capitalization of retained earnings or loans, he said.

Funds would also be committed in stages in line with project progress rather than paid in a lump sum, he said.

As Taiwan’s trade surplus with the US has widened, increasing energy purchases from the US could also help narrow the imbalance, Kung said.

Separately, asked about Pegatron Corp (和碩) chairman Tung Tzu-hsien’s (童子賢) suggestion of developing an artificial intelligence (AI) park in the Danhai New Town (淡海新市鎮) area of New Taipei City’s Tamsui District (淡水), Kung said it was “a pretty good idea.”

The area has advantages including large contiguous parcels of land, convenient transportation and access to labor, he said.

The Danjiang Bridge would also improve access to the Port of Taipei and provide links to Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, improving the area’s transportation advantages, he said.

In contrast, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) proposal to develop an AI park on the site of Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) could remain in the discussion phase for another decade because opinions remain divided, Kung said.

Taiwan’s AI industry cannot afford to wait for a consensus before moving ahead, he added.

data.title: Smartphone shipments crash 22% in worst quarter ever, research group says
data.description:
The smartphone market suffered its worst decline on record in the third quarter, after rising memory costs pushed global shipments down 22 percent year-on-year to 255.3 million units with worse to come, market researcher International Data Corp (IDC) said in a report released on Wednesday.

The higher cost of storage over the past year, led by demand from artificial intelligence industry orders, has hurt profitability across the mobile sector and forced companies to raise prices, cut back specifications and discard budget-focused models, IDC said.

Chinese brands like Xiaomi Corp (小米) and Oppo Mobile Telecommunications Corp (歐珀) took the worst hit among the top names, while Apple Inc and Samsung Electronics Co fared better due to their larger premium handset portfolios, the preliminary data from IDC’s Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker showed.

Device manufacturers are increasingly recognizing that they are facing a permanent structural shift and IDC expects market growth to be constrained through next year and any recovery in growth would not come until 2028 at the earliest, the report said.

As companies increase prices and push consumers toward flagship or high-end models, the long-term trend is seen translating into greater share of a smaller market for Apple and other vendors with large-scale distribution and a premium mix of products, it said.

“Current indicators suggest that the market has not yet reached the bottom,” IDC research director Nabila Popal said. “Memory costs have surged approximately 350 percent since last year and are still rising, creating substantial pressure on vendor margins and shipments. The worst is yet to come.”
